segments.text: When we talk about artificial intelligence, it helps to think of it as a giant calculator,
running math at a scale nobody can picture.
But that calculator can do some amazing things.
Recently, it helps solve a problem that challenged scientists for 50 years.
Inside your body, proteins act like tiny machines.
They carry oxygen, fight infections, and perform countless other jobs.
A protein's shape helps determine what it does, but figuring out those exact shapes
was incredibly difficult.
Then, an AI system called AlphaFold was introduced.
Through decades of experiments, scientists had determined about 200,000 protein structures.
AlphaFold predicted over 200 million protein structures, shared free.
Those millions of predictions give researchers around the world an immediate advantage.
They now have a clear starting point for studying complex diseases and developing new medicines.
Who actually helped make that scale possible?
To answer that, we look to the co-founder of DeepMind, Demis Hasavas.
Hasavas became a chess master at 13 and helped design the video game Theme Park at 17.
From there, he went on to study the brain and co-found the AI Lab DeepMind.
His team developed AlphaFold and chose to share its structure predictions completely free.
A kid who loved games helped solve a 50-year science problem.
More than 3 million people across over 190 countries have used those AlphaFold models.
That work led to Hasavas sharing the 2024 Nobel Prize in chemistry.
When he won, he explained his motivation.
I've dedicated my career to advancing AI because of its unparalleled potential
to improve the lives of billions of people.
This board outlines how AI is helping people stay healthy.
Starting on the left with finding cancer, doctors examine breast scans for signs of disease.
In a Swedish trial with over 100,000 women,
doctors using AI found more cancers than those without it.
Next is the Urgent Scans column.
A brain bleed requires immediate attention.
AI can flag a scan that shows a possible bleed so doctors can review it sooner.
Importantly, the process relies on human medical judgment at the end.
The doctor evaluates the scan and decides what care is needed.
Finally, we look at new antibiotics.
Because some bacteria resist many existing medications,
scientists need new options.
Researchers used AI to identify a Bousin,
which killed a type of drug-resistant bacteria in lab tests.
As the banner at the bottom summarizes, AI helps doctors find problems
and researchers find possibilities.
The benefits also extend out of the lab and into daily routines.
This board shows examples of helping people in everyday life.
Look at the Reading Allowed section.
A menu or food label presents a distinct challenge for blind people.
Today, AI tools on a phone can read the text
aloud and describe photos, helping with everyday tasks.
In the middle column, we have flood warnings.
These warnings give people critical time to prepare and move to safety.
AI helps provide free warnings days ahead,
including places without equipment that measures river levels.
On the far right is targeted spraying.
Farmers need to control weeds while strictly limiting chemicals
that can harm the environment.
AI guided equipment uses cameras to tell weeds from crops
and sprays where weeds are found.
These aren't abstract concepts for tomorrow.
As the board states, the upside is already reaching people.
Every one of those is true.
So the next time someone asks you,
what good does AI do for society?
You have an answer ready.
For starters, AI is accelerating work that protects and improves lives.
That brings us back to one more thing about Demis Hasabas.
His story doesn't begin in a lab.
It starts with a kid who loved chess and video games.
That level of brilliance is rare,
but the attitude is a choice that you can make starting today.
Whatever you happen to be good at,
point it at something that helps people.
You might not win the Nobel Prize,
but who are we to say you won't?
The big upside is happening today.
AI is already accelerating work that protects and improves lives.
